name: Vienna Smoke
lede: Vienna Smoke is a near-neutral charcoal grey, first recorded by Maerz and Paul in 1930 and named, like several of their plates, for a city rather than a pigment.

sections.title: A city name on a grey
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color first records this grey, plate 16 A 2, though the underlying plate traces back to 1902 [1]. The dictionary pairs it in the same small family as Phantom (1923) and Asphalt (1922), two other smoke-toned greys from the same plate block [1]. Nothing in our sources explains why Vienna specifically [1]; the name sits in the dictionary's run of place-and-mood names rather than a documented reference to the city's own smoke or stone.

Its nearest look-alike is [[davy-s-grey]], at a CIEDE2000 distance of only 2.7, with [[castor-grey]] and [[greyish-black]] close behind [2]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 33, chroma 1 and hue 91 degrees, essentially a neutral with only a faint warm cast [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this grey in 808 of 23,781 paintings (3.4%, as photographed), more common than 83% of the named colors we track [3]. It most often plays a mid-tone, in 48% of its 501 strongest matches [3]. Jacob Isaacksz van Ruisdael is its most devoted painter, at 5.3 times the baseline rate across his 18 works here [3]. The earliest dated match runs to 1225, seven centuries before the name's own 1930 record; the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the pigment existed then, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3].

origin.source: Maerz & Paul, A Dictionary of Color
